p.src: The mechanics of a relativistic particle must answer familiar questions in a new language. How does a particle move? What are its momentum and energy? Why do those quantities fit together into a four-vector, and how does $E=mc^2$ emerge from the ordinary machinery of mechanics? Before taking up those questions, we need one elementary approximation that will recur throughout the calculation.

p.src:
For any exponent $p$, the binomial series is $\begin{aligned}
(1+\epsilon)^p
&=1+p\epsilon\\
&\quad+\frac{p(p-1)}{2!}\epsilon^2\\
&\quad+\frac{p(p-1)(p-2)}{3!}\epsilon^3
+\cdots .
\end{aligned}$ The exponent may be positive, negative, fractional, or even complex. For sufficiently small $\epsilon$, the series converges rapidly and each successive term is smaller. We may then stop at whatever order the desired accuracy requires. The zeroth-order term is often the largest, but in the applications below it is frequently a constant and therefore dynamically uninteresting. The first correction is where the motion appears.

p.src:
We normally set $c=1$, so a velocity $v$ means the fraction $v/c$ of light speed. Take $\epsilon=-v^2$. With $p=\tfrac12$, $\sqrt{1-v^2}
=
1-\frac{v^2}{2}-\frac{v^4}{8}-\cdots
\approx
1-\frac{v^2}{2},
\qquad |v|\ll 1.$ With $p=-\tfrac12$, the two minus signs cancel: $\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-v^2}}
=
1+\frac{v^2}{2}+\frac{3v^4}{8}+\cdots
\approx
1+\frac{v^2}{2}.$ Many factors of $1/2$ in classical mechanics can be recognized, after the fact, as the first correction in one of these relativistic expansions. The approximation fails as $v$ approaches one; then no finite truncation captures the singular behavior of the exact expression.

p.src: What Counts as a Particle?

u.src: What Counts as a Particle?
en: What Counts as a Particle?

p.src: A particle in mechanics need not be elementary. It may be an electron, the Sun, a box of chocolates, or a donut. What matters is that the object holds together well enough for its overall motion to be described by a center of mass. A donut is a useful reminder that the center of mass need not lie in the material itself.

p.src:
In Newtonian mechanics the center-of-mass variables obey $\vec p=m\vec v,
\qquad
K=\frac12mv^2,
\qquad
\vec F=m\vec a.$ These formulas do not care whether the object is elementary or composite. A composite object also contains internal energy. A moving donut, for example, has center-of-mass kinetic energy plus chemical, thermal, and binding energy: $E_{\text{Newtonian}}
=
E_{\text{internal}}+\frac12mv^2.$ The internal term is independent of the overall center-of-mass velocity. Relativity will retain this distinction but will reveal that the internal energy contributes to the invariant mass of the whole object.

p.src: Plot a system’s position horizontally and time vertically. Its history is then a curve in spacetime. For one particle this curve is its worldline. The concept exists in Newtonian mechanics, but it becomes fundamental in relativity because Lorentz transformations mix space and time.

p.src: Timelike separation

u.src: Timelike separation
en: Timelike separation

p.src: If $(\Delta t)^2>\Delta\vec x^{\,2}$, then $(\Delta\tau)^2>0$ and the separation is timelike. There is a Lorentz frame in which the two events occur at the same spatial point. In that frame the line joining them is vertical and a clock can travel from one event to the other. Its elapsed reading is the proper time $\Delta\tau$.

u.src: If $(\Delta t)^2>\Delta\vec x^{\,2}$, then $(\Delta\tau)^2>0$ and the separation is timelike. There is a Lorentz frame in which the two events occur at the same spatial point. In that frame the line joining them is vertical and a clock can travel from one event to the other. Its elapsed reading is the proper time $\Delta\tau$.

p.src: Spacelike separation

u.src: Spacelike separation
en: Spacelike separation

p.src: If $\Delta\vec x^{\,2}>(\Delta t)^2$, the interval is spacelike. No inertial frame places both events at the same spatial point, but there is a frame in which they are simultaneous. Other frames can reverse their time order. Therefore neither event $A$ happened first nor event $B$ happened first is an invariant statement for a spacelike pair. This is the relativity of simultaneity in geometric form.

p.src: A massive particle has a timelike worldline: every sufficiently short segment satisfies $d\tau^2>0$. Successively composing velocities of $0.9c$ may bring a particle ever closer to $c$, but never beyond it. The approach resembles Zeno’s paradox. This causal restriction applies not only to material objects but also to signals and information, because information must be carried by physical systems. A faster-than-light signal would allow different frames to disagree about which end of its history is the cause and which is the effect.

p.src:
Ordinary velocity has three spatial components, $v^i=\frac{dx^i}{dt},
\qquad i=1,2,3.$ The relativistic velocity is obtained by dividing the full spacetime displacement by invariant proper time: $u^\mu
=
\frac{dx^\mu}{d\tau},
\qquad
\mu=0,1,2,3.$ Greek indices run over spacetime; Latin indices run over space. The zeroth component of position is $x^0=t$ in $c=1$ units, so $u^0=\frac{dt}{d\tau}.$

p.src:
To relate $u^\mu$ to $\vec v$, factor $dt^2$ from the interval: $\begin{aligned}
d\tau^2
&=dt^2-d\vec x^{\,2}\\
&=dt^2\left(1-\frac{d\vec x^{\,2}}{dt^2}\right)
=dt^2(1-v^2).\end{aligned}$ Taking the positive root for a future-directed worldline, $\frac{d\tau}{dt}=\sqrt{1-v^2},
\qquad
\frac{dt}{d\tau}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-v^2}}
\equiv\gamma.$ For a spatial component, $v^i
=
\frac{dx^i}{dt}
=
\frac{dx^i}{d\tau}\frac{d\tau}{dt}
=u^i\sqrt{1-v^2}.$ Thus $\boxed{
u^\mu
=
\gamma(1,\vec v)
},
\qquad
u^0=\gamma,
\qquad
u^i=\gamma v^i.$ At low speed $u^0\to1$ and $u^i\to v^i$. Near light speed both $u^0$ and the magnitude of the spatial four-velocity become large even though $|\vec v|<1$.

p.src: Recovering Lagrange and Newton

u.src: Recovering Lagrange and Newton
en: Recovering Lagrange and Newton

p.src:
Insert : $\begin{aligned}
L
&=-m\sqrt{1-v^2}\\
&\approx-m\left(1-\frac{v^2}{2}\right)\\
&=-m+\frac12mv^2.
\end{aligned}$ The constant $-m$ is independent of both position and velocity. It contributes the same amount to every path with the same endpoint times and therefore drops out of the Euler–Lagrange equations. The part with dynamical content is precisely $L_{\mathrm{Newton}}=\frac12mv^2.$ Thus the sign and mass normalization in the invariant action were chosen correctly.

u.src: From Three-Momentum to Four-Momentum
en: From Three-Momentum to Four-Momentum

p.src: A statement about one component of a four-vector is generally frame-dependent. For example, $\Delta\vec x=0$ says that two events share a position in one frame, but a boost tilts that interval and makes $\Delta\vec x'\ne0$. By contrast, $\Delta x^\mu=0$ is invariant: if all four components vanish in one frame, all four vanish in every frame. Likewise, $\vec u=0$ only identifies the particle’s rest frame; it is not an invariant description of the four-velocity.

p.src:
For a closed system, ordinary momentum conservation reads $\vec P_{\mathrm{initial}}-\vec P_{\mathrm{final}}=0.$ This is a three-vector equation. To make conservation manifestly Lorentz covariant, we need a fourth component that joins the three $p^i=mu^i$. The obvious completion is $p^\mu=mu^\mu.$ In $c=1$ units, $p^\mu=(p^0,\vec p)
=
m\gamma(1,\vec v).$

p.src:
Insert $p_i=m\dot x_i/\sqrt{1-v^2}$ and $L=-m\sqrt{1-v^2}$: $\begin{aligned}
H
&=
\frac{mv^2}{\sqrt{1-v^2}}
+m\sqrt{1-v^2}\\
&=
\frac{mv^2+m(1-v^2)}{\sqrt{1-v^2}}\\
&=
\boxed{\frac{m}{\sqrt{1-v^2}}}
=m\gamma.
\end{aligned}$ The cancellation is the key step. Comparing with $u^0=\gamma$, $H=mu^0=p^0.$ Thus the fourth component is the energy: $p^\mu=(E,\vec p),
\qquad
E=H
\qquad(c=1).$

p.src:
The exact energy and momentum diverge as $v\to c$: $\begin{aligned}
E&=\gamma mc^2\longrightarrow\infty,\\
\vec p&=\gamma m\vec v\longrightarrow\infty
\qquad(m>0).
\end{aligned}$ Reaching light speed would therefore require unbounded energy and momentum. A finite force acting for finite time supplies only finite impulse, so a massive particle can approach $c$ but cannot reach it.

p.src:
Suppose two particles move with equal and opposite momenta. Their total three-momentum vanishes, so we are already in the rest frame of the combined system. The invariant mass $M$ of that system is defined by its total energy in this frame: $Mc^2=E_{\mathrm{tot}}
\qquad
(\vec P_{\mathrm{tot}}=0).$ More generally, $M^2c^4
=
E_{\mathrm{tot}}^2-c^2\vec P_{\mathrm{tot}}^{\,2}.$

p.src: The invariant action was not chosen by guessing a force law. It was chosen as the simplest local Lorentz scalar that reproduces the Newtonian free-particle Lagrangian at low speed. Varying it gives $\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot x^i}\right)=0,$ so $\frac{dp_i}{dt}=0.$ For fixed nonzero mass this is equivalent to constant four-velocity: $\frac{du^\mu}{d\tau}=0.$ The worldline is therefore a straight line in spacetime. That single geometric statement contains both uniform speed and unchanging spatial direction.

Introducing charge and electromagnetic fields will be the next step beyond this free motion.
en: For now the force-free result is complete: a massive particle follows a straight timelike worldline, its invariant mass fixes the norm of its four-momentum, and energy and momentum are the four components of one conserved object. Introducing charge and electromagnetic fields will be the next step beyond this free motion.
